title: Prefix Caching Strategy Review - Acme Corp
summary: Technical deep dive focused on prefix/prompt caching strategy for multi-tenant workloads. Discussed cache key schemas, hit rate expectations, eviction and TTL strategies, isolation for VPC/on-prem, and how caching interacts with KV cache and batching. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share spec + perf numbers; Acme to provide sample prompt set and PII-sensitive patterns; schedule POC benchmark run and security review.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Zhou (Redwood SE), Carlos Diaz (Acme Platform Eng), Meera Anand (Acme ML/Infra), Tom Lee (Acme Security), Priya Shah (Acme PM)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood): alright everyone thanks for jumping on, um today we wanted to walk through our prefix/prompt caching approach and surface some of the tradeoffs for multi-tenant setups, especially for your VPC/on-prem plans
[00:18] Carlos (Acme): yep thanks Samir, high level we want to reduce token costs and tail latency for chat flows; our concern is safety across tenants and not leaking prefixes between customers
[00:35] Lena (Redwood): great, we'll start with the high-level split: prompt/prefix caching (application-level prefix reuse) versus KV cache which is the transformer key/value state for autoregressive generation. people confuse the two. prefix cache stores encoded activations or cached logits for fixed prompts; KV cache is runtime per-sequence attention state.
[01:02] Meera (Acme): quick question — does prefix cache store intermediate hidden states or just completions? how is it materialized?
[01:12] Lena (Redwood): good question. Redwood's prefix cache can be configured either to store token embeddings / encoder outputs and rehydrate them into the KV path, or to store pre-computed prompt encodings and short-circuit several decoder steps if the model and prompt match exactly. in practice we produce a serialized blob which includes a small header (model id, quantization profile, prompt hash) and then the encoded vectors. implementation details vary per backend (gpu vs on-prem CPU quantized).
[01:45] Tom (Acme): and encryption at rest? if these blobs contain anything that could be tied back to customer data we need them encrypted with our KMS key in the VPC option
[01:53] Samir (Redwood): yes, for private deployments we support customer-provided KMS; blobs can be encrypted per-tenant. hosted has tenant-scoped namespaces with app-level RBAC; we don't store raw PII. we'll note that in the spec.
[02:20] Carlos (Acme): walk us through the cache key schema you're proposing — what keys do you include to avoid accidental cross-tenant hits but still get reuse across users inside same tenant?
[02:33] Lena (Redwood): current recommended key: tenant_id || model_family || model_version || quant_profile || prompt_hash || prompt_version. optional: route or feature flag id if you need routing-based isolation. importantly we scope namespaces per-tenant in the KV store: even if a key collides, the namespace prevents cross-tenant reads. we also include a TTL and a size cap per-tenant so noisy tenants don't evict everything.
[03:05] Meera (Acme): prompt_version? how do we handle small prompt edits that should still hit?
[03:12] Lena (Redwood): that's a common tension. exact match hashing is simple but brittle. we offer fuzzy prefix matching logic — tradeoff is correctness vs complexity. we can canonicalize prompts (normalize whitespace, redact variable fields like timestamps, optional template placeholders) and then hash. for semantic fuzzing we can use a short semantic fingerprint with a higher miss risk. we recommend starting with normalized exact-hash and iterating.
[03:45] Carlos (Acme): any metrics from other customers on hit rates for common chat workloads? numbers we can baseline against?
[03:51] Samir (Redwood): yes, across several SaaS customers we see 25-45% prefix-cache hit rates on templated flows; for heavy multi-turn assistants with many unique user prompts it drops below 10%. biggest wins come from templated prompts (welcome flows, transactional templates). we'll share the benchmark spreadsheet after the call.
[04:20] Priya (Acme): how does batching interact with cache hits? does cache lookup add latency that defeats the batching gains?
[04:30] Lena (Redwood): good nuance. cache lookup is a constant-time key-value read — on a well-provisioned backend it's sub-ms. batching benefits happen during token-generation where multiple sequences are combined to reuse kernels. if prefix cache short-circuits N tokens the effective batch shape changes; we have dynamic batching that adapts. worst-case: cache lookup adds a small per-request overhead but still reduces total token work. in our perf numbers we see median latency drop even with lookup cost.
[05:10] Tom (Acme): we need to ensure multi-tenant safety for on-prem installs where Acme runs a single cluster with multiple internal namespaces. what's the recommended isolation model?
[05:21] Lena (Redwood): for private deployments we support two models: per-tenant isolated caches (separate Redis/rocks instances) or shared store with strict namespace + envelope encryption. isolated caches are simplest for security but costlier. shared store with tenant encryption and access controls is more cost effective. for compliance customers we usually recommend dedicated per-tenant namespaces backed by customer-managed disks and KMS.
[05:55] Meera (Acme): eviction strategies? LRU, LFU, size tiers? we have some high-cardinality ephemeral prompts
[06:03] Lena (Redwood): we support policy layers: per-tenant capacity caps, weighted LRU with frequency boosting for templates, and TTLs with sliding windows. also we segment caches into hot prefix shards (small, high-turnover) vs cold blob store (larger, compressed). if you have ephemeral traffic patterns we can set short TTLs for certain prompt classes.
[06:35] Carlos (Acme): quantization — any effect on cache portability? if we quantize the model or change kernel selection, do cached blobs become invalid?
[06:45] Lena (Redwood): yes, include quant_profile in the cache key. a cache blob produced with int8 kernels might not rehydrate correctly for a float16 runtime. Redwood's cache metadata tracks model_version, quant_profile, kernel_config and rejects mismatched blobs. we also keep small compatibility layers where we can rescale embeddings in some cases, but we don't recommend relying on that.
[07:12] Samir (Redwood): another operational note — rolling upgrades and model rollouts. we tag blobs with rollout_id so can selectively invalidate or prefer new blobs during canary. avoids serving stale behaviour post-rollout.
[07:30] Meera (Acme): observability — what metrics should we track to feel confident?
[07:36] Lena (Redwood): key metrics: cache hits/misses per model per-tenant, hit-rate by prompt template, latency delta (with vs without cache), bytes saved, token reduction, eviction rates, and top keys evicted. we also surface per-tenant cost-savings estimates. we can emit tracing spans for cache read/write times so you can spot cold-start storms.
[08:05] Priya (Acme): on data residency — if a blob contains parts of a prompt with PII, is it safe?
[08:12] Samir (Redwood): design principle is to avoid storing raw PII. canonicalization should scrub known slots (emails, phone numbers) if customers want. if you need absolute assurance, turn off prompt caching and rely on KV cache which is ephemeral per-request and never persisted off encrypted disk in private installs.
[08:37] Tom (Acme): audit logs — we need read/write audit trails for cache access for SOC2. can you log per-tenant cache reads without leaking prompt contents?
[08:45] Lena (Redwood): yes, we log metadata events (key accessed, tenant id, latency) not the blob contents. for hosted customers we emit logs to configured sinks; for private we can forward logs to your SIEM. logs include request id and a non-reversible key fingerprint so you can correlate without storing plaintext prompts.
[09:10] Carlos (Acme): performance tradeoffs — give us an example: 2ms lookup vs 50ms token generation saved — is that realistic?
[09:18] Lena (Redwood): yes, for medium-sized models a 50–200 token skip can save tens to hundreds of ms depending on kernel throughput. our numbers: avg cache lookup 0.5–2ms on Redis cluster, token gen per token ~8–25ms depending on model and quant. so template-heavy flows see big wins.
[09:45] Meera (Acme): what about memory pressure on GPUs when rehydrating prefixes?
[09:52] Lena (Redwood): rehydrating embeddings/kv states uses GPU memory; we stream where possible but for very large prefixes you might see memory bumps. we support offloading large prefix blobs to host memory and async prefetch into GPU for scheduled workloads. runtime has heuristics to cap prefix length for in-GPU rehydration.
[10:20] Samir (Redwood): let's talk hit-rate modeling — we recommended you provide sample traffic distribution so we can simulate. for example if 30% of prompts are from 10 templates, we can target 30–40% hit rate. without templating, hit rates fall off quickly.
[10:45] Carlos (Acme): ok we'll prepare that. any recommended TTL values to start with?
[10:50] Lena (Redwood): starts: templates 24–72h, session-scoped prefixes 10–60m, ephemeral prompts 0–5m. adjust based on eviction rates and observed reuse.
[11:10] Priya (Acme): POC idea — run our baseline chat workload on your hosted test cluster with prefix caching enabled/disabled and share cost/latency delta
[11:18] Samir (Redwood): yes that's exactly what we propose. typical POC cadence: ingest sample prompt set, run synthetic replay at 1x/5x traffic, measure hit rates, latency percentiles, and token savings.
[11:40] Meera (Acme): can the cache key include conversation context id so that intra-conversation prefix reuse is prioritized?
[11:47] Lena (Redwood): yes, include conversation_id as optional dimension for intra-session reuse. but that narrows reuse across users. a hybrid key works: session flags + template id.
[12:05] Tom (Acme): for on-prem security, we want to ensure the cache store can't be read by other processes. any recommended OS-level protections?
[12:12] Lena (Redwood): run cache on dedicated nodes, use file-system-level encryption, lock down network ACLs, require mTLS to access cache endpoints, and use process-level isolation. we include a hardening checklist in the security appendix.
[12:35] Carlos (Acme): who owns cache invalidation when templates change? our product team may update a template and expect cache to invalidate quickly
[12:43] Samir (Redwood): templates should bump prompt_version; our SDK has hooks to send invalidation events to the cache (by key prefix) or to set a short TTL on that template's keys. we support pub/sub invalidation for near-real-time.
[13:05] Meera (Acme): any examples of accidentally serving a wrong template because of fuzzy matching?
[13:12] Lena (Redwood): rare but possible with semantic fingerprinting. that's why sensitive workflows should use exact canonicalization. fuzzy is opt-in and we recommend a manual review step when enabling fuzzy mode.
[13:35] Priya (Acme): can we see a demo of the cache ops, like hits/misses per tenant?
[13:40] Samir (Redwood): yes we can show the Redwood Console dashboards in follow-up. Lena will include relevant dashboard screenshots.
[14:00] Carlos (Acme): any other pitfalls — e.g., cold-start storms after deploy?
[14:06] Lena (Redwood): yes, deploy-time cold starts can cause a temporary spike in work. mitigate with warmers, preheat common templates, and progressive rollout. our rollout tooling can prioritize warming keys on new nodes.
[14:35] Meera (Acme): about the benchmarking spreadsheet you mentioned — will it include per-model breakdowns and quant profiles?
[14:42] Samir (Redwood): yes, we'll provide per-model, per-quantization profile numbers including average per-token latency, cache lookup latency, and simulated hit-rate savings.
[15:00] Tom (Acme): security follow-up — can we get a short write-up on how tenant encryption, audit logs, and key rotation work for private installs?
[15:06] Samir (Redwood): yes, we'll include a security appendix and a proposed config for your environment.

[Segmented transcript: mid call more detailed technical exchange]
[22:00] Lena (Redwood): deep dive — when we rehydrate KV states into the attention layers we must keep alignment of position ids; if the cached prefix used different positional encoding because of off-by-one, generation diverges. we store position metadata and canonicalize position offsets in the blob.
[25:40] Meera (Acme): quant detail — when int8 is used some activations are clipped; does that affect reconstruction of cached embeddings?
[25:50] Lena (Redwood): small effects possible. that's why quant_profile must be part of the key. for safety we invalidate cross-quant blobs. we can sometimes store full-precision metadata to allow safe up-scaling but that's heavier.
[29:10] Carlos (Acme): monitoring — can you emit per-tenant cost-savings estimates into our billing system?
[29:18] Samir (Redwood): yes we can export aggregate token reductions and estimated $ saved; for private installs we can integrate via webhooks or CSV export.

[40:00] (longer discussion on eviction algorithms, shards, and failure modes — some transcription noise)
[41:12] Speaker 3: ummm something about rolling back the cache?
[41:20] Lena (Redwood): if a rollout causes bad outputs we have automatic fallback: disable cache by header, fallback to older model version, and we can blacklist keys produced during the bad window.

[49:30] Samir (Redwood): ok to recap — action items: we'll send spec and spreadsheet; you'll send prompt corpus; we'll schedule POC perf run; security to get appendix. any other asks?
[49:48] Carlos (Acme): include hit-rate examples for templated vs freeform and note recommended TTL defaults
[49:55] Priya (Acme): please include sample invalidation API calls we can wire into our UI
[50:02] Samir (Redwood): noted. thanks everyone, we'll follow up over email with calendar invites for the POC slot.
[50:20] (meeting closes, minor crosstalk)

Notes: transcript contains occasional imperfect words and speaker misattributions typical of automated transcription. references: Redwood prefix caching spec (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/prefix-cache - placeholder), benchmark spreadsheet (to be shared), security appendix (attached in follow-up).
competitor_notes: Customer mentioned Anthropic and OpenAI as alternative providers; discussion focused on price/latency tradeoffs and on-prem features compared to managed vendors.
